questions.q: Added value is…
o: the price minus the cost of bought-in materials
questions.why: It measures what the business adds to its inputs.

questions.q: A social enterprise…
o: has social or environmental aims and reinvests profit to meet them
questions.why: It can make profits but uses them for its social purpose.

questions.q: Which is an internal stakeholder?
questions.why: Internal stakeholders are within the organisation: employees, managers, owners.

questions.q: A business has revenue of $500 000. It spends $320 000 on bought-in materials and services and $100 000 on wages. What is its added value?
questions.why: Added value = revenue − cost of bought-in materials and services = 500 000 − 320 000 = $180 000; wages are paid out of added value, not deducted to find it.

questions.q: A government privatises its state-owned railway company. What is the most likely change in the business's main objective?
o: From earning profit to providing a free service
From serving shareholders to serving only the government
No change, because the same managers remain
From providing a public service to earning a return for private shareholders
questions.why: Once in the private sector the business is owned by shareholders, who usually expect profit, which may conflict with unprofitable public services.

long.q: Explain two differences between a private limited company and a public limited company.
scheme: B1: a public limited company can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange
B1: a private limited company can only sell shares privately, with the agreement of other shareholders
B1: a public company must publish more detailed accounts
B1: so it can raise much more capital but risks takeover

questions.q: Herzberg's hygiene factors…
o: cause dissatisfaction if absent but don't motivate
questions.why: Motivators include recognition, responsibility and achievement.

questions.q: Labour turnover is…
o: the percentage of staff leaving in a period
questions.why: (Number leaving ÷ average number employed) × 100.

questions.q: Which motivation theory separates hygiene factors from motivators?
questions.why: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but don't motivate.

questions.q: A business had an average of 250 employees during the year and 30 of them left. What is its labour turnover?
questions.why: Labour turnover = staff leaving ÷ average number employed × 100 = 30 ÷ 250 × 100 = 12%.

questions.q: A manager breaks jobs into simple tasks, pays workers per item produced and supervises them closely to raise output. Whose ideas does this approach reflect?
questions.why: Taylor's scientific management assumed workers are motivated mainly by money and favoured simple tasks, piece rates and close control.

long.q: Explain two non-financial methods a manager could use to motivate employees.
scheme: B1: one method, e.g. job enrichment / job rotation / empowerment / team working
B1: explained, e.g. more responsible, varied work meets higher-level needs (Maslow, Herzberg's motivators)
B1: a second method, e.g. recognition / training / delegation
B1: explained, e.g. employees feel valued, so effort and retention rise

questions.q: In the product life cycle, sales grow fastest during…
questions.why: Sales rise rapidly as the product gains acceptance.

questions.q: Market segmentation means…
o: dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs
questions.why: Segments can be based on age, income, location or lifestyle.

questions.q: What does a price elasticity of demand of −0.4 mean?
o: Demand is price inelastic, so raising price raises revenue
questions.why: Apply it: say what it means for this business's revenue.

questions.q: A firm raises its price from $20 to $22 and quantity demanded falls from 1 000 to 850 units. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.why: PED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price = −15% ÷ +10% = −1.5, so demand is price elastic.

questions.q: A holiday company designs separate packages for thrill-seekers and for customers who value luxury and relaxation, whatever their age or income. Which type of segmentation is this?
questions.why: Psychographic segmentation groups customers by lifestyle, attitudes and personality rather than by age, income or location.

long.q: Explain two elements of the marketing mix a business could use to launch a new smartphone.
scheme: B1: one element identified, e.g. price (penetration or skimming)
B1: explained in context, e.g. skimming earns high profit from early adopters
B1: a second element, e.g. promotion (social media, influencers) or place (online and retail)
B1: explained in context, e.g. reaching young buyers where they shop

questions.q: Capacity utilisation is…
questions.why: High utilisation spreads fixed costs; very high leaves no slack.

questions.q: Just-in-time inventory management aims to…
o: receive inputs only as they are needed
questions.why: It cuts storage costs but depends on reliable suppliers.

questions.q: Why does more output not guarantee more profit?
o: Goods may not be sold, and extra output adds costs
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common assumption was that more output guarantees more sales and profits.

questions.q: Which best describes kaizen?
o: Holding large buffer inventories in case demand rises
Continuous small improvements, often suggested by the workers themselves
Producing goods only when an order is received
questions.why: Kaizen is a lean production approach in which many small, ongoing changes, usually from employees, improve quality and efficiency.

questions.q: A hotel has 80 rooms and on average 60 are occupied each night. To reach 90% capacity utilisation without adding rooms, how many rooms must be occupied on average?
questions.why: 90% of the maximum capacity of 80 rooms = 0.9 × 80 = 72 rooms.

long.q: A factory can make 5000 units a month and makes 3500. Calculate its capacity utilisation and explain one problem of operating at this level.
scheme: B1: fixed costs are spread over fewer units, so the average cost per unit is higher (or idle resources, lower morale)

questions.q: Working capital is…
questions.why: It funds day-to-day operations.

questions.q: Profit and cash differ because…
o: sales on credit count as revenue before cash is received
questions.why: Timing differences mean a profitable business can run out of cash.

questions.q: Which is a full definition of fixed costs?
o: Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many gave only a partial definition such as 'costs that do not change'.

questions.q: What is a cash-flow forecast used for?
o: Predicting future cash inflows and outflows to spot shortfalls
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates continue to believe cash-flow forecasts calculate profit.

questions.q: Net cash flow is calculated as:
questions.why: Examiners (2023): errors often came from subtracting inflows from outflows rather than the other way round.

questions.q: ARR uses which figure for investment?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not calculate the average investment and so got the ARR wrong.

long.q: A business has fixed costs of $24 000 a month. It sells its product for $20 and the variable cost is $12 a unit. Calculate the break-even output and the margin of safety when it sells 4000 units.
scheme: M1: contribution per unit = $20 − $12 = $8
A1: break-even = 24 000 ÷ 8 = 3000 units
M1: margin of safety = 4000 − 3000
A1: = 1000 units

long.q: A business has current assets of $45 000, of which $15 000 is inventory, and current liabilities of $30 000. Calculate its current ratio and acid test ratio.
scheme: M1: current ratio = 45 000 ÷ 30 000

questions.q: A SWOT analysis looks at…
questions.why: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats external.

questions.q: Ansoff's matrix: selling new products in new markets is…
questions.why: It is the riskiest strategy.

questions.q: Investment appraisal: net present value accounts for…
questions.why: Future cash flows are discounted to present values.

questions.q: An option costs $50 000 and has a 0.6 probability of earning $100 000 and a 0.4 probability of earning $20 000. Using a decision tree, what is the net expected value?
questions.why: Expected value = 0.6 × 100 000 + 0.4 × 20 000 = $68 000; subtracting the $50 000 cost gives $18 000.

questions.q: A firm aims to have the lowest costs in its industry so that it can compete on price across the whole market. Which of Porter's generic strategies is this?
questions.why: Cost leadership targets the broad market with the lowest unit costs; focus targets a niche, and diversification is an Ansoff growth option, not a Porter strategy.

long.q: Evaluate whether a business should use Porter's generic strategies to compete in a new overseas market.
scheme: B1: cost leadership, differentiation or focus explained
B1: applied to the business's strengths and the market
B1: limits: hybrid strategies, local conditions
B1: a supported judgement

long.q: A project costs $50 000 and returns $15 000 a year for five years. Calculate the payback period and the average rate of return (ARR).
scheme: A1: = 3.33 years (3 years 4 months)
M1: average annual profit = (75 000 − 50 000) ÷ 5 = 5000
